# Slicing heuristics

## Finding vertical outcomes

- Phrase every candidate slice as "<actor> can <do something observable> end to end". If the
  sentence needs a system noun as its subject ("the API supports...", "the schema stores..."),
  the cut line is wrong — regroup until an actor is the subject.
- Start from the change's Intended Product Outcome and split along user-visible capability, not
  along the artifacts' file layout.
- The thinnest useful version of a behaviour is a better first slice than a complete one: one
  journey path working beats every path half-working.
- A slice may span several requirements, and a large requirement may span several slices. The
  unit is the coherent increment; requirements are what it declares coverage against.
- Each slice's `verification` must be demonstrable without the other slices (except those it
  `depends-on`): something a reviewer can exercise and observe in product terms.

## Anti-patterns to reject

- Layer slices: "database slice", "backend slice", "frontend slice". Three layer-slices produce
  nothing verifiable until all three land — the exact failure slicing exists to avoid.
- Endpoint slices and screen slices: surfaces, not outcomes.
- One-slice-per-requirement by reflex: mirrors the requirements list instead of cutting along
  outcomes; often couples every slice to every other.
- Dependency chains that encode a technical build order. `depends-on` is for one increment
  genuinely building on another's product outcome; a linear chain of every slice is a smell.
- A "final integration slice" that makes everything work: it means the earlier slices were not
  vertical.

## Partial coverage vs splitting a requirement

- Prefer `coverage: partial` with a precise `scope` when a large requirement naturally serves
  two outcomes: keep the requirement whole (stable ID, one acceptance context) and let each
  slice state exactly which part it covers, plus which slice covers the rest.
- Splitting the requirement itself is a Product Change decision, not a slicing decision — only
  propose it when the two halves have genuinely different acceptance criteria, and route it back
  through the change, never through slice files.
- A vague scope ("part of FR-X") is a validation error in spirit and blocks promotion in
  practice: promotion needs to know what was actually covered. Name the flows, rules or cases
  the slice includes and excludes.
